transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Sara Patel (Redwood SE), Jamal Rivera (Redwood SE), David Nguyen (Horizon - Dir ML), Priya Kapoor (Horizon - Platform), Michael Lee (Horizon - CTO), Lina Park (Horizon - SRE)

Summary / Topics (auto-gen): discussed throughput numbers from last week, continuous batching hot paths, observed queueing under burst traffic, proposed cap-and-adapt approach to concurrency, agreed next runs and artifacts.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining on time, uh quick roll call?
00:07 David Nguyen: David here, Priya, Michael, Lina are on our side.
00:10 Priya Kapoor: yep hi all, Priya here.
00:12 Alex Chen: great. Sara, Jamal from our side?
00:15 Sara Patel: Sara here.
00:16 Jamal Rivera: Jamal here, ready.
00:18 Alex Chen: cool, agenda for 30-45. Quick recap of last benchmark, dig into the continuous batching behavior we saw, talk concurrency targets and queueing, then agree next steps.
00:28 David Nguyen: sounds good. we saw a weird thing where throughput plateaued around 850 rps at 8k tokens average, p99 spiked to 720ms in the afternoon burst.
00:38 Sara Patel: yeah that aligns with our logs; we saw batching depth increase and then some requests waited in queue for a few hundred ms. there might be a threshold where kernel selection flips and latency jumps.
00:50 Priya Kapoor: we are running the redwood dedicated cluster with 4xA100-ish nodes, pinned model to r-instruct-13b-q4 and qkv cache enabled. we had concurrency target at 200.
01:04 Jamal Rivera: right, and one nuance: continuous batching will try to fill batches up to N or until latency SLO. if bursts happen, you either see more big batches (good for throughput) but if the device gets saturated, queueing increases p99.
01:20 Michael Lee: can you explain the flip you mentioned, Sara?
01:23 Sara Patel: sure, so there are two optimization regimes - up to a certain sequence-length distribution and batch size the runtime uses a fused kernel path. beyond that the kernel selection changes, memory or kernel scheduling causes tail-latency to step up. it's not deterministic, it's workload-proportional. sometimes a single large batch pushes us into a slightly different memory layout and we see p99 go up.
01:44 Lina Park: we also noticed CPU spikes on the host during those times. do you think it's pre/post-processing or the runtime?
01:50 Jamal Rivera: likely both; pre/post tokenization threads plus the runtime's memory copy patterns. we should capture a flame and the host metrics aligned with that run.
01:57 Alex Chen: ok quick walk through the numbers from last week's run - i have the spreadsheet. we had sustained throughput 700-850 rps depending on time windows; avg latency 120-180ms, p95 ~340ms, p99 up to 720ms in high-concurrency windows. concurrency was set to 200, effective batching averaged 6-8 tokens per batch, maximum observed batch size 32.
02:25 David Nguyen: is that per-GPU? our monitoring shows per-node saturation around 0.85 utilization.
02:30 Sara Patel: that's overall, per node varied. some nodes had hot shards because we didn't evenly spread KV-cache hot keys; smart routing could help.
02:39 Priya Kapoor: we had sticky sessions for certain clients which pushed hot prefixes.
02:42 Jamal Rivera: sticky prefixes will blow up batching distribution skew; continuous batching loves diverse prefixes because it packs more, but if many requests share common prefix, the KV-cache becomes hot and that shard takes longer.
02:56 Michael Lee: so what's the recommended knob? lower concurrency? raise it?
02:59 Sara Patel: two levers: cap concurrency so you avoid queue buildup, and adjust the continuous batching timeout (aka max latency target for batch formation) so that small batches are emitted quicker under tail pressure. also configure adaptive batching thresholds per model/profile.
03:16 Alex Chen: in practice we recommend a cap-and-adapt: set a conservative concurrency cap (e.g., 120) then enable adaptive-batching that lowers the accumulation window when device latency goes above X ms, then gradually allow concurrency to float up if p99 stays within SLO.
03:33 David Nguyen: any quick math for us for our target of 1k rps? currently we hit 850 at best.
03:36 Jamal Rivera: rough calc: throughput ~ (concurrency * tokens_per_request) / avg_latency_in_seconds. so to get 1k rps at same tokens and latency you'd need more concurrency or lower latency. but the knee of efficiency is batching: if we can increase average batch packing without pushing kernel flip, we can move up.
03:56 Priya Kapoor: we tried increasing batch window to 40ms and saw better throughput but p99 jumped.
04:02 Sara Patel: that's the tradeoff. another approach is to set a max_batch_size at runtime to prevent those huge batches that flip kernel, and pair that with more aggressive batching timeout so you don't stall.
04:14 Michael Lee: can we do queueing/backpressure at the proxy level? we want to avoid large queuing delays on the client side.
04:19 Alex Chen: yes, you can use concurrency targets and token-budget based rate limiting at the ingress. Redwood's routing supports per-route concurrency caps and token-weighted queues so upstream clients see 429s or backpressure instead of huge tail latency.
04:33 Lina Park: would 429s break our SLAs for the app? we need to be careful.
04:37 David Nguyen: ideally the app can retry with jitter and not escalate on user-facing calls. for internal batch jobs we can allow retries or longer timeouts.
04:45 Priya Kapoor: what about KV-cache warm/cold effects? we saw a step-change after a cache purge window at 03:00 UTC and throughput dropped.
04:54 Jamal Rivera: cache warmth matters a lot. cold KV accesses amplify per-request latency because we pull large key blocks. we recommend staggered pre-warm runs and a read-through cache warming step in the POC. also track eviction rates.
05:10 Sara Patel: for your next benchmark we propose a graded run: keep model pinned to r-instruct-13b-q4, run three phases - warmup (20m low-rps), steady low concurrency (cap 100 for 30m), steady high concurrency (cap 180 for 30m) and then a burst window. collect per-request batch size distribution, kernel selection logs, per-node CPU/GPU utilization, KV-cache hit rates, and host-level traces.
05:36 David Nguyen: that sounds good. what tooling do you need from our side?
05:39 Alex Chen: ideally we get the logs to the shared S3 with timestamps and we get access to the Grafana query links. Jamal will enable KV-cache tracing on the next run and Sara will provide the kernel selection markers so you can correlate.
05:52 Priya Kapoor: can you show an example config we should apply to cap concurrency and adjust batch windows?
05:57 Sara Patel: yes i uploaded a sample config snippet to the shared drive, but quick example: 
06:02 Sara Patel (cont): concurrency_limits: 120; batching: {max_latency_ms: 25, max_batch_size: 24, adaptive: true, p99_target_ms: 300}. Also enable backpressure_mode: token_weighted_queueing, and set ingress retry policy: 3 attempts with exponential backoff.
06:25 Michael Lee: will that reduce throughput vs current run?
06:28 Jamal Rivera: initially maybe slightly lower peak but much tighter p99; with tuning you can recover throughput without the p99 spikes. it's safer for user-facing workloads.
06:36 David Nguyen: any quick wins we can do now?
06:38 Alex Chen: three quick wins: 1) cap concurrency to 120, 2) set max_batch_size to 24, 3) enable KV-cache pre-warm and stagger traffic to avoid hot shards. we'll include the exact CLI/helm snippet.
06:52 Priya Kapoor: ok we'll try that in our next run. please include the sample helm/daemonset flags.
06:58 Sara Patel: will do. also we'll include a script to parse the batch-size distribution from the runtime logs.
07:05 Michael Lee: about costs - if we reduce concurrency and increase stall, how does that effect our billing?
07:10 Alex Chen: cost is primarily GPU time; if you run longer but with better packing you may not increase cost proportionally. Redwood Optimize will give you an estimate - we'll include an updated cost spreadsheet reflecting the recommended config.
07:22 David Nguyen: competitor question - how does this compare if we tried AWS Bedrock or an OpenAI managed endpoint?
07:27 Jamal Rivera: Bedrock has less model-level kernel control and you can't tune batching at this granularity; OpenAI offers simplicity but limited batching controls; Redwood Dedicated gives you per-model config, kernel-level profiling, and KV-cache control which is why many infra teams prefer it for predictable p99 and cost tuning.
07:44 Priya Kapoor: ok that helps.
07:47 Alex Chen: to recap next steps: Alex will share updated throughput spreadsheet and config by tomorrow; Sara will share kernel/batching analysis; Jamal will enable KV-cache tracing; Priya will run the graded benchmark and upload logs. we'll reconvene next Wed for a deeper review.
08:05 Michael Lee: one more ask - can we get a short doc explaining the kernel flip behavior and what metrics to watch?
08:10 Sara Patel: yes short doc + example Grafana alerts (p99, avg batch size, max_batch_size hist) i'll attach.
08:17 David Nguyen: perfect. thanks team.
08:20 Alex Chen: thanks everyone, i'll send calendar invite for 2026-12-16 15:00 PST.
08:24 Meeting end.
